_note:
ACT 4, BEAT 2: RECORDS.

This floor belongs to the capital's author and it is full of people doing real work -- forecasting, relief, conservation, a man on resonance who says the Aurelian rings were never built to push, and two archivists at the back. Nothing here overrides any of that: Act 4 puts Lyra and Tarin into the archive at the back and lets the shelving do the rest.

They are SPAWNED rather than placed on the map, so that this floor's own cast stays entirely the capital author's, and because spawnNpc dedupes by id -- if the two of them are ever added to the map under these ids nothing here changes or doubles up.

Lyra goes straight through to the archive without waiting, which is in character and is the only signpost this beat needs.

The respawn script below is what puts them back when the player wanders off and comes back, which canon's freedom-between-beats rule requires. Only the first 'enter' script that starts is run, so order in this file matters: the once-only arrival first, the respawn second.

lines: Forecasting, relief and conservation along the front, and a long room at the back with a rail across it.
Somebody two desks over is eating an apple and writing at the same time.
Ninety of the people on this floor are conservation and relief.
They are the reason the lights are on and I would like you to have counted them.
Nobody has looked at us.
Nobody has ever needed to.
That is what I have been trying to say since the ridge and I have never had the words for it.
She goes through to the stacks at the back without waiting for either of you.
The archivist looks up, and does not ask her for anything.

_note: Puts the two of them back on any later visit while the act is still running. No onceFlag: it is meant to run again.

Lyra and Tarin, at the west end of the two reading aisles between the stacks, which is where the beat is.

THE TILES ARE MEASURED, NOT CHOSEN. Each aisle on this map is a corridor between two runs of shelving, open at x=15, x=16, x=23 and x=24 and walled by bookcases in between, and NPCs are solid. Standing Lyra on 16,13 sealed the aisle at the west end while the map's own archivist sealed it at the east, and the reading shelf in the middle became unreachable -- the first run of the Act 4 driver walked at it for two hundred steps and gave up. 15,13 leaves 16 open, so the player walks past her to the shelf and turns round to talk to her, which is also the better staging.

THE TRUTH ABOUT ELIAS, part one: the file anybody could have asked for.

Fires along the reading aisle between the two runs of shelving at the back, four feet from the archivist, whose own line -- written by the capital's author -- is that a file may leave this room for the Director's office and nowhere else. The sewn sleeve at the back of this folder is stamped for exactly that, which is what hands the next scene to Lyra.

Four boxes and a stamp: nine years of service, a sailing date, a one-page manifest with the word MISSING in it, and a loss report that says weather. All of it true, all of it public, and all of it wrong in a way that nothing in the folder can show. The junior archivist upstairs has already told the player, without knowing what he was telling them, that a loss report with no assessor's name means nobody went and looked.

lines: Lyra has written the request out in pencil, the way the rail says to.
The archivist has put the folder on the reading shelf and gone back to his chair.
ELIAS. Nine years.
Field archaeology. Then Deep Survey. Then Deep Survey again, at his own request.
Signed onto the survey vessel CORVANE on the eleventh.
Sailed on the fourteenth.
Recovery manifest. One page.
ONE ITEM RECOVERED. ONE ITEM LOGGED. ONE ITEM NOT RETURNED TO STORE.
That is the page she read.
That is the whole of what she read, and she got theft out of it.
Loss report. The CORVANE went down forty miles west of the Tideglass approaches.
All hands. Cause given: weather.
There is no assessor's name at the bottom of it.
The junior archivist told you on the way in what that means. Nobody went and looked.
It is a thin folder for nine years of a man.
He said that too. He said they mostly are.
There is a sleeve sewn into the back board, and it has a stamp on it.
HELD. NOT TO BE ISSUED.
RELEASE TO THE DIRECTOR'S OFFICE ONLY. CROSS-REFERENCE 4A.
{name}. Go and stand next to Lyra and do not say anything.
Let her get there on her own. She will get there.

_note:
THE TRUTH ABOUT ELIAS, part two, and the moral shape the whole act is built to protect.

CANON, EXACTLY:
  - Elias tried to leave with the Tideheart because he had worked out what it was for.
  - A Meridian commander sabotaged his vessel -- the same commander the player met in
    the Sanctum in Act 3, so that it is a face and not a job title.
  - CASSIAN DID NOT ORDER IT. He found out afterwards and covered it up rather than lose
    the programme. That is what makes him guilty, and the distinction is the character.

The evidence has to survive a vessel lost with all hands and no body, so it is not the wreck: it is a shipyard night book from the evening before she sailed, a fitter's statement taken three days after, and one unsigned sheet in Cassian's own hand written ninety-two days later. The storm was real. That is the reason for doing it this way, and Tarin says so out loud -- somebody opened a valve and then let the weather finish it, in a game whose whole subject is the weather.

The sheet is the most important document in the game and it is four lines long. The last of them -- that he is writing it down so that he cannot later tell himself he did not know -- is the whole man. Somebody who lies to himself can be argued out of it. He took that exit out on purpose and has lived eleven years without it.

WHY LYRA CAN OPEN IT. She is not a director. She has signed her father's name on Foundation paper since she was fourteen because he asked her to, to save himself an hour a day. The thing he trusted her with is the thing that opens the sleeve, and she has never used it before. That is her cost, paid here, and it is why she is the one who is betrayed rather than the one who is angry.

Sets aur_deep_open, which is this map's own flag for the west stair guard, and removes him live, because hiddenIfFlag is only read when a map loads.

lines: West stair. There is a floor under this one and I have never been on it.
Fifteen when I started here, and I did not know there was a floor under this one.
The request slip is in. It is on the reading shelf between the stacks.
I am not going to read it to you. He was not my father.
Show me the stamp.
Cross-reference 4A is the yard book.
That is not an archaeology reference. That is a shipyard.
She has gone very still, and her voice has not changed at all, which is how you can tell.
Yes.
I know. I have not had to for a year and it has made me nothing but stupid.
You say nothing.
She works out what you are doing, and she is not grateful for it.
I have signed his name on Foundation paper since I was fourteen. He asked me to.
It saves him an hour a day and he has never once checked what I put it on.
I have never used it for myself. Not once, for anything, in three years.
I would like somebody in this room to have heard me say that.
Two letters and a line under them.
She does not look at the page while she is doing it.
A shipyard night book, copied out and stamped.
The CORVANE, in the yard, on the night of the thirteenth.
BALLAST TRUNK OPENED 23:10. TWO HOURS. CLOSED 01:05.
FOUNDATION PARTY. ONE NAME ON THE LINE.
C. KELL.
She stood four feet away from you in that room.
She told you she thinks about him every day and you thanked her for it.
A fitter's statement, taken by the yard three days after the loss.
He says the sea-cock linkage had been adjusted while he was off the boat.
He says he was told not to enter it in the book.
He says he did not, and that he has thought about it every week since.
The storm was real.
That is the clever part, {name}. The storm was real.
Somebody opened a valve and then stood back and let the weather do the rest of it.
The last thing in the sleeve is a single sheet, unheaded, in a hand that is not a clerk's.
It is dated ninety-two days after the CORVANE.
I have read this twice, and then I have read her expenses for that week,
and she was in the yard.
I did not ask her to. I would have said no.
I am as certain of that as I am of anything, and it does not help.
If this leaves the building the programme ends inside a month,
and everything that would have come after it ends with it.
I have weighed the two.
I am writing it down so that I cannot tell myself later that I did not know.
It is not signed. It was never sent to anybody.
It has been in a sewn sleeve in this room for eleven years, filed by the man who wrote it.
That is his hand.
I have four hundred of his letters. That is his hand.
She has not sat down, and she has not put the sheet down either.
No. He did not.
And I have just watched myself be relieved about that,
in front of you, about your father, and I would like very much to be sick.
He wrote it down so that he could not pretend afterwards.
That is the worst line on the page and it is the one I would have expected.
Somebody who lies to himself can be argued out of it.
He took that door out on purpose and he has lived eleven years without it.
Nobody says anything for a while.
Two aisles over, somebody laughs at something, and it goes on being an ordinary Thursday.
He worked out what they were going to do with it, so he took it out of the room.
That is not theft. That is the only sane thing in the whole folder.
There is a floor under this one.
I have worked in this building since I was fifteen and my pass does not open it.
His does. And I can sign his name,
and it turns out that I am going to keep doing that today.
The man on the west stair reads the countersign twice, and then stands out of the doorway.
He looks relieved. It cannot have been a good posting.
I keep waiting to feel like we have caught somebody.
It has not turned up. It is not that kind of building.
A sewn sleeve with a stamp on it, in a room where nothing leaves.
Somebody wanted that findable and unreadable at the same time. Think about who.
Ask everybody on this floor everything. We have passes and they are all bored.
That is the only two things you need in a records office. I have read a book.
